safety.title: The cloud asks. The robot decides.
safety.body: Qafila Fleet never moves a robot on its own authority. Every motion request passes through the robot's own gate, which checks the lease, the link and the STOP latch. Lose the link and the robot stops by itself.
safety.evidence: In our field tests, both Go2 quadrupeds stopped in under 1 second in all 6 walking link-cut trials (October–November 2026).

hero.title: The platform
hero.lead: Qafila Fleet has four parts: a command center for the whole fleet, missions, a shared Fleet Brain and safety rules that live on the robot. Each part is marked with what exists today.

command.title: Fleet command center
command.lead: One screen for every robot, whatever its maker.
command.fleetBody: A card per robot with online state, link, motion, battery and agent version. Open a robot for its details, its missions today, its settings and its timeline.
command.cameraBody: Each online robot's camera streams through the robot's own gate. The tile gets a short-lived, view-only token; it can never drive.
command.controlTitle: Take control with a lease and an authenticator code
command.controlBody: One operator holds a robot's control lease at a time. It ends after 30 seconds without a keepalive, and ending it locks motion. Enabling motion needs an authenticator (TOTP) session and a named check: a spotter, the remote in hand, the area clear. An admin can take over, with a reason that is logged.
command.actionsBody: Buttons such as Stand, Sit or Recover are drawn from each robot's profile. They stay off until motion is enabled, and they go to the robot through its gate, never from the cloud.
command.profilesBody: Turn robot features on or off per robot. Only what the robot class supports can be enabled, every change is logged, and the robot gets its settings each time it connects.
command.incidentsBody: Rules open and close incidents for link lost, offline, low battery, unsynced clock and expiring credentials, and can post each one in English and Arabic to Slack or Telegram.
command.capsuleBody: A 24-hour timeline per robot. Pick a moment to see the link, motion, who held control, battery, open incidents, logged events and, where turned on, a camera snapshot.
command.wallBody: A read-only fleet screen with live cameras for an operations room. It opens with a viewer link that expires and can be revoked; it has no controls.
command.copilotBody: Ask questions in plain language about incidents, the audit log, missions and the timeline. Its tools only read. It can run on your own model server.

missions.title: Missions across many robots
missions.lead: Today the platform records what each robot did. Planning one mission across several robots is the next step.
missions.todayTitle: Today: mission log, daily figures and fleet map
missions.todayBody: The platform turns the skills a robot reports into a mission log with daily figures per robot: missions done and aborted, STOPs, link losses, time moving and distance. The fleet map shows robot positions and named places on a site map. These pages only observe; they send nothing to a robot. Skill reporting from the robots is still being wired in, so the log fills in as robots start sending it.
missions.nextTitle: In development: one mission, many robots
missions.nextBody: An operator sets a goal once, and the platform splits it across robot types: a drone looks from above, a quadruped goes closer, a humanoid works with what people use. Every new mission needs an operator's approval before it runs.

brain.title: Fleet Brain
brain.lead: Each robot learns. The cloud shares it with every robot.
brain.body: A robot builds knowledge where it works: maps, named places, what it saw and where. Fleet Brain collects that knowledge in the cloud and shares it with every robot that can use it, so a robot that has never been to a site starts with what the fleet already knows.
brain.status: Fleet Brain is the platform's direction and is in development. It is not part of Qafila Fleet today.
brain.diagramLabel: Diagram: robots send what they learn to Fleet Brain in the cloud, which shares it back with every robot.
brain.loopLabel: Animated diagram: a robot learns on site, an operator reviews what it learned, and Fleet Brain shares it with every robot. Then the loop repeats.
brain.loopLearnBody: A robot maps a site, names places and notes what it saw.
brain.loopReviewBody: An operator checks what it learned before anything is shared.
brain.loopShareBody: Fleet Brain sends it to every robot that can use it.

safety.title: Safety by design
safety.lead: The robot keeps STOP, the lease and the gate. The cloud never goes around them.
safety.p1Title: Lose the link, the robot stops
safety.p1Body: The robot watches its link to the platform itself. When it is lost, the robot stops and stays locked until an operator enables it again.
safety.p2Body: A command that is not renewed runs out, so a lost message can never keep a robot moving.
safety.p3Body: STOP from any source is accepted at once and holds until the next Enable.
safety.p4Body: Operator, mission or on-robot assistant: only the current lease holder can move the robot.
safety.p5Body: After a restart the robot comes online with motion off. Only an operator can turn it on.
safety.p6Body: Sign-ins, leases, enables, takeovers, tokens and setting changes all go to the audit log.
safety.evidence: Field tests, October–November 2026: both Go2 quadrupeds stopped in under 1 second in all 6 walking link-cut trials. We describe how robots stop; we do not promise zero risk.
safety.diagramLabel: Diagram: the cloud sends requests; the gate on the robot checks the lease, the link and the STOP latch before anything reaches the motors.

security.title: Security
security.lead: Built for a fleet that moves in the real world. Only what runs today is listed as available.
security.robotBody: Link watch, STOP latch, lease check and the gate run on the robot. A robot starts locked and stops when its link drops.
security.transitBody: Robots and operators talk over a private WireGuard network (Tailscale or self-hosted Headscale). The dashboard and every robot gate use HTTPS with certificates for their own names.
security.rolesBody: Viewer, operator and admin roles. Admin sign-in and enabling motion need an authenticator code (TOTP); failed sign-ins share one limit.
security.tokensBody: Each robot token is signed and bound to one robot, one operator and one lease, and expires within minutes.
security.auditBody: Every sign-in, lease, enable, takeover, token and setting change is recorded, with who and when.
security.networkBody: A robot can reach the control plane and nothing else. No unauthenticated endpoint can move a robot.
security.updatesBody: The robot installer pins every download by SHA-256 and installs Tailscale from its signed package repository.
security.signedBody: Signed, verified updates of the Qafila agent itself.
security.secretsBody: Secrets live in environment files, never in code and never in logs.

integrations.title: Works with
integrations.lead: Open standards and tools your team already uses.
integrations.i1Body: Every robot runs a ROS 2 stack in a container; the vendor operating system stays untouched.
integrations.i2Body: Go2 connected today; G1 integration in progress.
integrations.i3Body: Drones and ground vehicles through MAVROS. In development.
integrations.i4Body: Incident alerts by webhook, in English and Arabic.
integrations.i5Body: The copilot uses any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, such as Ollama or vLLM on your own server.
integrations.i6Body: A private fleet network, hosted or self-hosted.

hero.title: Humanoids, quadrupeds, drones and ground vehicles. One platform.
hero.lead: Every robot class gets the same fleet page, the same control flow and the same safety rules. Here is where each class stands today.

quadruped.title: Quadruped
quadruped.does: Crosses rough ground, stairs and tight spaces that wheels cannot.
quadruped.connects: Qafila agent on the robot, ROS 2 stack in a container, a gate in front of every control and camera stream.
quadruped.state: Connected to Qafila Fleet. Link-loss stop tested on both of our Go2s.

humanoid.title: Humanoid
humanoid.does: Works where people work: doors, stairs and tools made for human hands.
humanoid.connects: Same agent and gate, Unitree's official ROS 2 interface, action definitions for its own buttons.
humanoid.state: In simulation and gantry tests. Not yet available for onboarding.

drone.title: Drone
drone.model: In-house, Raspberry Pi 5 with an ArduPilot flight controller
drone.does: Sees from above: roofs, towers and wide sites.
drone.connects: Agent on the companion computer, ArduPilot through MAVROS, with the flight controller's own failsafe as a backstop.
drone.state: Tested in simulation (ArduPilot SITL). Indoor tests next; outdoor flights only with a permit.

ground.title: Ground vehicle
ground.model: In-house, Raspberry Pi 5 with a motor board and 2D LiDAR
ground.does: Carries sensors along routes it measures and maps.
ground.connects: Same agent, ArduPilot Rover through MAVROS, a physical emergency stop.
ground.state: Tested in simulation (ArduPilot SITL). Hardware build in progress.

byo.title: Bring your own robots
byo.body: Qafila Fleet is not tied to one maker. Each robot class is described by a profile: what it can do, which buttons it gets and how it stops when the link drops. Adding a class means writing its profile and its driver, not changing the platform.
byo.tbd: [TBD] list of further makers and models, once each one is tested.

hero.title: Connect a robot in minutes
hero.lead: Four steps from a robot on your bench to a robot you control from the fleet page. The robot is never able to move until an operator says so.

how.step1Body: In the dashboard, open Add robot and enter its name, class and network host. You get one command. Nothing is created and no key is issued yet.
how.step2Body: From the operator workstation, the command installs the Qafila agent on the robot, joins it to the private fleet network and enrols it with its own credential. The robot maker's system software stays untouched.
how.step2Code: Example of the command the dashboard shows
how.step3Body: The robot appears on the fleet page with its link, camera and incidents. It starts locked: motion is off.
how.step4Body: Take the control lease, sign in with your authenticator code and confirm the safety check: a spotter, the remote in hand, the area clear. Then enable motion. STOP always wins, and if the link drops the robot stops.
how.archLabel: Diagram: on the robot, the Qafila agent and a gate sit next to the robot stack. They talk to the Qafila Fleet control plane over a private network. Operators and wall screens use the control plane in a browser.
how.aCloudSub: fleet page, leases, incidents, audit, copilot

story.title: Why Qafila

hero.title: Developers
hero.lead: Qafila Fleet has an HTTP API, JSON Schema contracts for robots and one onboarding command. Here is how a robot gets from your bench to the fleet.

developers.s1Body: From the operator workstation. Installs the agent, joins the private network and enrols the robot. It comes online locked.
developers.s2Body: Sign in with your password and authenticator code, then read the fleet.
developers.s3Title: Take the lease and enable motion
developers.s3Body: Take the robot's control lease, then enable motion with the lease and a named safety check. Keep the lease alive with renew; when it ends, motion locks.
developers.codeNote: Examples. Replace the host, robot id and credentials with your own.
developers.apiBody: Versioned under /v1: sign-in, robots, enrolment, credentials, network, settings, control lease, enable and disable motion, and robot tokens. Every motion route needs a signed-in operator.
developers.contractsBody: JSON Schemas for the agent messages (heartbeat, telemetry, arm and disarm, settings, robot events) and for robot capabilities and actions. A robot's buttons in the dashboard are drawn from its actions file.
developers.sdkBody: A kit for writing a driver for a new robot class, on top of the robot contracts.
developers.docsTbd: [TBD] public documentation link. Today the API reference and contracts are shared with pilot partners on request.
